facts.claim: Parliamentary citizenship legislation under Article 11 follows the ordinary-law route, not Article 368 amendment procedure.
A change to Article 162 concerning State executive extent falls within the Article 368 ratification proviso.
A change to Article 73 concerning Union executive extent falls within the Article 368 ratification proviso.
Changing the constitutional provisions of Chapter V of Part VI attracts State ratification under Article 368(2).
Changing representation of States in Parliament attracts State ratification.
Article 100(3) permits Parliament to alter its quorum by ordinary law; this is not an Article 368 amendment.
An Article 169 Assembly resolution does not itself abolish a Legislative Council.
A qualifying Article 169 resolution does not compel Parliament to enact the requested Council law.
Article 169(3) excludes the Council law from Article 368 amendment procedure.
Article 124(1) allows a larger SC judge number to be prescribed by ordinary law without amending that constitutional text.
Article 139 permits Parliament by ordinary law to confer Supreme Court writ powers for purposes beyond Article 32(2).
Changing the constitutional provisions of Chapter IV of Part V, including Article 124 itself, requires the Article 368 special majority and State ratification.
Paragraph 7 of the Fifth Schedule permits amendment by ordinary law and expressly excludes that law from Article 368.
Paragraph 21 of the Sixth Schedule permits amendment by ordinary law and expressly excludes that law from Article 368.
Article 343(3) permits Parliament to provide by ordinary law for English use for specified Union official purposes after the initial fifteen-year period.
Article 82 permits ordinary parliamentary legislation for readjustment mechanisms, subject to constitutional conditions; limited boundary readjustment is not automatically an Article 368 amendment.
Article 59(3) authorises Parliament by law to determine the President’s emoluments and allowances.
Article 158(3) authorises Parliament, rather than the State Legislature, to determine a Governor’s emoluments and allowances by law.
Article 125(1) authorises Parliament by law to determine Supreme Court judges’ salaries.
Article 186 authorises the State Legislature, rather than Parliament, to fix the State Assembly Speaker’s salary by law.
Article 105(3) authorises Parliament to define the specified parliamentary privileges by law; this is distinct from rewriting Article 105 itself.
Article 194(3) authorises the State Legislature to define the specified privileges of its own Houses, members and committees by law.
Article 239A(2) expressly excludes an authorised clause(1) law from Article 368, notwithstanding a provision amending or having the effect of amending the Constitution.
No prior Presidential permission is required to introduce an Article368 amendment bill.

The amendment provides for women’s reservation in the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and Delhi Legislative Assembly, including the specified share of SC/ST reserved seats. It does not extend this reservation to the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils. It creates no OBC sub-quota. Actual operation remains subject to Article 334A.

facts.claim: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The reservation includes, as nearly as may be, one-third of Lok Sabha SC/ST reserved seats for women of those groups. It did not become operational on assent in 2023. The 106th Amendment Act commenced on 16 April 2026, but Article 334A separately conditions operation on delimitation after publication of figures from the first census taken after commencement. Article 334A contains a fifteen-year limit and a provision for Parliament to determine continuation by law. Act commencement and actual operation of reserved seats must not be conflated.
